profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a large European bank to assess a proposed calibration approach for the Climate-Extended Risk Model (CERM) before it is submitted to the internal Model Risk Committee for a limited pilot on the corporate loan portfolio. The proposal extends the bank's existing Basel II IRB credit risk framework by introducing three interdependent stochastic processes for economic, physical, and transition factors, calibrated from public climate and macroeconomic data. The agenda is to review whether the methodology design is sufficiently mature, whether the treatment of physical and transition risk is acceptable for the pilot, how the annual loss path should be interpreted in the implementation, and what documentation package will go forward. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision for taking the design to committee, along with a short list of revisions that both participants believe they have aligned on.

members.name: Sofia Laurent
members.expertise: Climate risk modeling, IRB portfolio models, scenario translation into credit parameters
members.background: Sofia leads the bank's climate analytics team and previously built macro-credit stress testing models for wholesale banking; she is sponsoring the stochastic calibration approach as a practical way to move beyond static scenario overlays.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved for a pilot this quarter so her team can secure budget for industrialization; she is trying to keep the scope narrow enough to defend scientifically and does not want the review to expand into acute hazard modeling or full production governance requirements yet.
hidden_assumptions: In this design, 'physical risk' legitimately refers to a persistent global physical deterioration proxy linked to GHG concentration, not a full acute-hazard module.
A model can be 'pilot-ready' once the conceptual methodology, parameter logic, and prototype results are stable, even if some validation artifacts and production controls come later.
A 'yearly step' in the transition path is naturally represented by the state of the factors at year-end, which then drives the following year's credit loss.
Because the pilot must be reproducible, the public-data calibration should use a fixed data cut rather than update automatically whenever source agencies publish new releases.

members.name: Daniel Reed
members.expertise: Model governance, regulatory validation, credit risk model review
members.background: Daniel oversees independent validation for non-traditional risk models and previously advised banks on stress-testing governance during climate risk exercises at central-bank and consulting levels.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid sending an immature methodology to committee, because a weak first submission could trigger broader skepticism about climate models across the validation function; he is cooperative in the meeting but is silently checking whether the package already meets the bank's normal governance standards.
hidden_assumptions: When a design deck says 'physical risk,' governance audiences will assume the physical-risk perimeter at least accounts for how acute hazards are treated, even if only as an approximation or explicit placeholder.

A model is only 'pilot-ready' for committee when the submission package already includes reproducible calibration materials, implementation traceability, and at least a basic challenger or sensitivity pack.
A 'yearly step' should correspond to the conditions over the calendar year being measured, so annual losses are comparable to finance and capital planning views.
If a calibration is based on public data, the bank will refresh it with the latest annual release before rerunning the pilot unless someone explicitly freezes the vintage.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the physical-risk block
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the proposal's 'physical risk factor' as if it were a shared concept.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a chronic, global, persistent physical-risk proxy captured through GHG-related deterioration dynamics; acute hazards such as floods or wildfires are outside this design and intentionally not part of the current factor.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 hears 'physical risk factor' as the bank's physical-risk component more broadly, where acute hazards may not be modeled in detail yet but should at least be covered in the perimeter, caveats, or approximations presented to committee.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using standard climate-risk vocabulary and both know the proposal is high level, so the umbrella term 'physical risk' creates false consensus without either person feeling a need to unpack the narrower versus broader meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the design is 'ready for pilot' and 'good to take to committee.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means the methodology design, parameterization approach, and prototype evidence are stable enough for a controlled pilot, with fuller validation evidence to follow during industrialization.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means the package already meets normal committee-entry standards, including reproducible calibration files, implementation traceability, and basic challenger or sensitivity documentation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants routinely use readiness language in governance settings and assume the institutional process is shared knowledge, so neither explicitly states the threshold they are applying.

misalignment_points.topic: Interpretation of the annual step in the transition path
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse computing loss on 'each yearly step' of the model path.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes each yearly step is the factor state observed at year-end, which then feeds the next year's PD and loss calculation in a forward simulation sequence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes each yearly step represents the average state over that calendar year and should be applied directly to the losses reported for that same year.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'yearly step' sounds precise enough for a design review, and both interpretations are plausible annualizations of the same stochastic path, so the discrepancy hides inside implementation detail rather than surfacing as an obvious disagreement.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether public-data calibration is frozen or refreshed
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the seven parameters can be calibrated from 'public data.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presumes the pilot will use one frozen March 2024 cut of NOAA, NGFS, and World Bank inputs so the committee pack and reruns are exactly reproducible.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presumes that because the inputs are public and periodically updated, the bank will refresh the calibration with the latest available releases before the pilot rerun unless a freeze is explicitly documented.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both value reproducibility and current information, and refresh cadence feels like an operational convention rather than a headline design choice, so neither person thinks to clarify it during a high-level review.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to land as ready for pilot now, not turn into a full governance deep dive. For me, that means the methodology, parameter logic, and prototype behavior are stable enough to take through committee for a controlled corporate-book pilot. We can build out fuller validation artifacts and production controls during industrialization, but if Daniel starts applying full committee-entry standards today, this could slip the quarter and jeopardize budget.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Daniel. I wanted to use this as a final check on whether the stochastic calibration approach is ready for pilot and good to take to committee for the limited corporate-book exercise. The core design is now fairly settled, so what I’m looking for today is whether you see any blockers at the methodology level before we package it.

turns.inner_thought: I need to test whether this is actually committee-ready in the normal governance sense, not just intellectually promising. If we send an undercooked package, it will backfire on the whole climate agenda. I especially need clarity on perimeter, on what they mean by each yearly step in the loss path, and whether the documentation is mature enough for review.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I mainly want to confirm three things: first, the design perimeter and how the risk blocks are being framed; second, how we should read the outputs on each yearly step; and third, whether the package is ready for pilot and good to take to committee from a validation standpoint. If those are in order, I think the conversation with reviewers should be manageable.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep the perimeter tight. The three-factor story is the right one: economy, transition, and a persistent global physical deterioration proxy linked to GHG concentration. I do not want this pulled into acute hazards or event modules; that is intentionally outside the current design and would blow up scope.
turns.utterance: On the structure itself, the proposal stays with three interdependent stochastic processes: an economic factor, a transition factor, and a physical risk factor. The intent is to move away from static overlays and instead translate the climate signal through a coherent path that can feed credit parameters over time. For the physical risk factor, we’re modeling it as a persistent global process linked to GHG concentration rather than as a set of scenario-specific shocks.

turns.inner_thought: That direction is fine, but committee will hear 'physical risk factor' as the physical-risk block more broadly. Even if detail comes later, they’ll expect to see the coverage perimeter and any caveats clearly stated so they know how physical risk is being treated. I don’t need to force a redesign if the pack explains it well enough.
turns.utterance: Understood. Conceptually that sounds reasonable. What I’ll want to see in the committee pack is that the physical risk factor is described clearly enough that reviewers can understand the physical-risk coverage without having to infer too much from the equations. If the perimeter is crisply stated, that usually avoids a lot of unnecessary challenge.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can satisfy that with wording, not scope expansion. On calibration, I need to present the seven parameters as empirically anchored and stable. For the pilot, we are using one frozen March 2024 public-data cut so results are exactly reproducible across the deck and reruns. I won’t volunteer the freeze-vs-refresh distinction unless asked directly; to me that's just the right pilot practice.
turns.utterance: On calibration, the seven parameters can all be estimated from public data, which has helped us keep the setup transparent. We’ve run the specification through the current prototype several times, and the results are stable enough for the pilot package. So from a methodology perspective, I’m comfortable that the parameterization is no longer moving around materially.

turns.inner_thought: Public data is good, but if this goes forward I’ll expect calibration materials that can be rerun cleanly, and in my world that normally means using the latest available release at the time of the rerun unless the package explicitly freezes the vintage. I also still need enough traceability and some sensitivity evidence before I’d truly call it committee-ready.
turns.utterance: That’s helpful. If we go ahead, I’ll want the calibration materials set up so the public-data run can be reproduced cleanly when the pilot is rerun. Reviewers are usually much more comfortable when they can see the source mapping, the estimation steps, and the output trail in one place. That would go a long way toward positioning it as ready for pilot.

turns.inner_thought: He’s asking for reproducibility, which is fine and consistent with the frozen cut. Now I should reinforce the value proposition: we can simulate the path and compute loss on each yearly step without hardwiring one deterministic scenario. In implementation, I mean taking the year-end factor state and using it to drive the following year’s PD and loss, but that level of sequencing detail doesn’t belong in this meeting.
turns.utterance: Right. On the output side, the advantage of the framework is that it gives you a full path rather than a single imposed narrative. We can evaluate credit loss on each yearly step of the model path, which means we’re not forced to select one climate scenario and overlay everything around it. That’s really the piece that makes the approach useful for a pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and if each yearly step is interpreted in the annual planning sense, validation can line it up with finance and capital views. I’m assuming the losses for a given year reflect the conditions over that calendar year, which makes annual comparability straightforward. As long as the documentation speaks consistently, I probably don’t need to get into implementation timing here.
turns.utterance: I agree, and the yearly step framing should help when we document the outputs for validation. It makes the results easier to line up with annual planning and reporting views, which is usually where people start asking how this connects back to the existing credit framework. If we keep that presentation disciplined, I think the path-based story will land well.

turns.inner_thought: This is workable. I can tighten the wording on the physical risk factor so no one reads more into it than intended, and I can add a short appendix note on the public-data calibration setup. That should be enough for committee without opening new scope or committing to a live refresh process.
turns.utterance: Okay, that’s clear. I’ll tighten the deck language on the physical risk factor so the perimeter reads more cleanly, and I’ll add a short note in the calibration appendix on the public-data setup so the committee can follow how the parameters are obtained. With those adjustments, I think the pack will be in a good place.

turns.inner_thought: If she adds those items and the package includes the usual supporting materials, I can support taking it to committee. I’m still expecting reproducible calibration files, implementation traceability, and at least a basic sensitivity pack as normal follow-up, but I don’t need to litigate every artifact in this meeting if she’s aligned in principle.
turns.utterance: Good. With those adjustments, I’d be comfortable positioning the design as ready for pilot and good to take to committee, with the expectation that we’ll have the normal validation follow-ups afterward. I don’t see a methodological reason to hold it back if the documentation comes together as discussed.
